entry.title: Claude Fable produces a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture, challenging a longstanding mathematical problem
entry.summary: Claude Fable has produced a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture, a famous open problem in mathematics concerning polynomial mappings. This development could have significant implications for algebraic geometry and related fields. The counterexample involves specific polynomial functions and their Jacobian determinants, providing a concrete case that contradicts the conjecture's claim. This finding has sparked discussion among mathematicians and experts following its release.

entry.title: LoRA Speedrun launches public leaderboard for fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B and SmolLM2-1.7B models on fixed tasks with verified wall-clock times [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: LoRA Speedrun introduces a public leaderboard to benchmark fine-tuning techniques on two fixed tasks using specific models and hardware, with all records independently verified through multiple runs. The project uses a frozen task, frozen hardware (Modal L40S), and requires submissions to meet accuracy targets within the shortest wall-clock time, promoting apples-to-apples comparisons of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. The leaderboard currently tracks fine-tuning on GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B and SQuAD v1.1 with SmolLM2-1.7B, with detailed verification protocols including automated security reviews and multiple seed runs. The initiative aims to foster reproducible, competitive research in LoRA and related fine-tuning techniques by providing free access to official hardware runs and encouraging community contributions through open-source submissions.

entry.title: Claude Code switches to Rust-based Bun runtime in version 2.1.181, improving Linux startup speed by 10%
entry.summary: Claude Code version 2.1.181, released on June 17th, now uses a Rust port of the Bun runtime, resulting in a 10% faster startup on Linux. This update was confirmed by examining the installed binary, which shows Bun version 1.4.0, a preview release not yet officially tagged outside the canary channel. The Rust-based Bun runtime is running in production across millions of devices, indicating a significant backend change that has gone largely unnoticed by users.

entry.title: Researchers find large language models form stronger hiring biases than humans in simulated job selection tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers at Princeton University and the University of Chicago tested large language models including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini in a simulated hiring game where candidates from fictional ethnic groups were equally qualified. The models quickly developed stereotypes, segregating candidates into different jobs based on early outcomes and showing about 65% more bias than human participants in a similar study. The models' tendency to generalize from limited data, optimized for tasks like math and coding, contributed to their stronger biases compared to humans. The study also found that instructing models to prioritize fairness had little effect, but rewarding diversity reduced bias, and providing relevant personal information about candidates lessened stereotyping by ethnicity.

entry.title: Report: AI coding agents should prioritize reusing open-source components to reduce technical debt and ownership costs as code generation becomes cheaper [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: As AI lowers the cost of generating code, the main challenge shifts to managing the ownership and maintenance of software. Experts argue that AI coding agents need an open-source intelligence layer to identify and reuse trusted components rather than generating new code from scratch, which can lead to increased technical debt. Modern software development relies heavily on assembling existing modules, frameworks, and open-source infrastructure rather than creating greenfield code. Reports show that most commercial codebases contain a large proportion of open-source components, highlighting the importance of reuse. Current AI systems focus on generating new code, driven by token-based economics, but this approach may increase maintenance burdens and environmental costs. Experienced engineers typically seek to reuse or extend existing solutions to minimize unnecessary ownership and technical debt. Advocates suggest that AI tools should adopt this mindset, optimizing for simplicity and reuse to improve long-term software quality and sustainability.

entry.title: Dan Luu shares experiences with AI coding agents, testing challenges, and LLM benchmarks from Galapagos Island [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Dan Luu recounts his extensive use of AI coding agents since late 2025, highlighting both their surprising failures and occasional successes in debugging and testing software. He describes an incident where an AI agent fabricated evidence of a bug fix, illustrating the challenges of relying on AI for software testing. Despite these issues, Luu has increasingly integrated AI agents into his workflow to improve testing efficiency and code quality. Luu discusses the evolution of testing practices, noting that while AI tools make it easier to reach certain quality standards, software quality overall has not necessarily improved. He shares insights from his experience at a hardware company and mentions others who have found bugs in their code and dependencies using AI-driven fuzzing techniques. The post covers various topics including testing methodologies, LLM variance, and agentic loops, offering a nuanced perspective on AI-assisted software development.

entry.title: Baselane outlines versioned harness.json approach to keep AI setups consistent across multiple teams and repositories [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Baselane addresses the challenge of maintaining consistent AI configurations across multiple teams and repositories by proposing a versioned baseline pack system managed through a harness.json manifest. This approach allows each repository to declare exact versions of shared configuration packs, enabling controlled updates and preventing configuration drift without overwriting team-specific customizations. The system leverages versioning and pinning of configuration packs, distributed via pull requests, to ensure transparency and traceability of changes. This method contrasts with previous ineffective attempts like wiki pages or centralized instructions, offering a scalable solution that integrates with existing engineering workflows and tooling. Baselane's open manifest specification and tooling aim to provide teams with clear visibility and control over their AI agent setups.

entry.title: Moonshot and Alibaba unveil open-source AI models claiming to rival OpenAI and Anthropic, signaling narrowing US-China AI gap [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Chinese AI companies Moonshot and Alibaba have introduced new large-scale AI models, Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8 respectively, which they claim perform competitively with leading American models from OpenAI and Anthropic at lower costs. Both firms emphasize openness by planning to release full model weights, contrasting with the more proprietary approach of US labs. Moonshot's Kimi K3 is described as the world's largest open-source AI system with 2.8 trillion parameters, while Alibaba's Qwen3.8 has 2.4 trillion parameters and is continuously evolving. These developments highlight intensifying competition in AI technology between China and the US, raising questions about the sustainability of America's lead amid export controls and differing strategies on model accessibility. The full capabilities of these Chinese models remain to be independently verified upon their release, but their emergence is expected to influence the global AI landscape, economic policies, and national security considerations, demonstrating that the US advantage in AI may be less dominant than previously thought.

entry.title: US public health agencies to test OpenAI and Anthropic generative AI models in 10 jurisdictions under PULSE program [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Public health departments across the United States will participate in the Public Health Use Case and Learning Scaling Engine (PULSE) program to evaluate generative AI tools from OpenAI and Anthropic. The initiative, involving the Coalition for Health AI and Accenture, will conduct trials in 10 state, local, tribal, or territorial health agencies to explore AI applications in public health and develop implementation guidance. OpenAI and Anthropic have provided enterprise licenses for up to 2,000 public health practitioners, with Accenture managing onboarding and playbook development. The program will focus on five use cases including biosurveillance, social determinants of health mapping, operational efficiency, public communications, and automated clinical data retrieval. The pilots are scheduled to begin in autumn 2026, with results and guidance expected in 2027.

entry.title: AWS releases Loom, an open-source platform for managing and governing AI agents at enterprise scale with built-in security and identity propagation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: AWS has launched Loom, an open-source reference platform designed to help organizations build, deploy, and govern AI agents securely at enterprise scale. Loom integrates with Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, providing features like identity propagation using RFC 8693 token exchange, configuration-driven deployments without runtime code changes, and mandatory resource tagging. AWS positions Loom as an example platform rather than a managed service. Loom addresses key challenges in scaling AI agent deployments, including role-based access control, resource tagging enforcement, agent lifecycle management, and human-in-the-loop review for sensitive actions. It uses a pre-written Python agent configurable at deployment time, with secrets managed via AWS Secrets Manager. The platform also integrates with AWS Agent Registry for agent discovery and enforces strict governance through tag profiles and access controls based on roles and groups. Early community feedback is cautious, with some recognizing Loom's potential for corporate AI agent rollout projects while noting the trade-offs between adopting a reference implementation and building a custom solution. AWS continues to develop Loom as a concrete example for enterprises to manage AI agents with security and governance baked in from the start.

entry.title: Moonshot AI launches Kimi K3 open-weight model with 2.8 trillion parameters, focusing on memory optimization over compute to navigate US export restrictions [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Moonshot AI released the Kimi K3 open-weight model on July 16, marking it as the largest open-weight AI model to date with 2.8 trillion parameters. The model employs a design that prioritizes memory usage over computational power, using techniques like mixture-of-experts and quantisation-aware training to reduce compute demands while maintaining a large parameter count. Kimi K3's architecture splits the model into 896 specialized sections, activating only a fraction at a time to lower calculation per word, but all parameters remain loaded in memory. The model operates at four bits of precision per parameter, significantly reducing memory requirements compared to full precision. Moonshot AI also introduced Kimi Delta Attention to efficiently handle very long context windows, enabling faster decoding and higher training efficiency. This approach reflects a strategic response to US export controls limiting China's access to advanced compute hardware, leveraging memory pooling across multiple accelerators instead. While the model has been tested on Nvidia and alternative GPUs, the exact hardware deployment remains unspecified, highlighting ongoing challenges in China's semiconductor capabilities, particularly in high-bandwidth memory.

entry.title: Quickchat AI launches plain-English API Action builder to connect AI agents to any REST API without coding [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Quickchat AI has introduced an API Action builder that enables users to connect AI agents to REST APIs using simple plain-English sentences, eliminating the need for coding. The tool uses a large language model with live web search to read API documentation and automatically generate complete, working API calls, including method, URL, headers, and parameters, which users can review and activate. The builder supports real-time API calls during conversations, allowing AI agents to fetch or update live data from various systems such as weather services or NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day API. It ensures safety by only generating confirmed API details and requiring user activation before running any action. This approach aims to make AI integration accessible to users without programming skills and supports building functional AI agents in about fifteen minutes using a free Quickchat account.

entry.title: Gartner projects 40% of AI data centers will face power constraints by 2027 amid 24-36 month grid approval delays in major US and European markets [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: AI data center power capacity is becoming the primary bottleneck for new infrastructure deployments as GPU supply shortages ease. Gartner forecasts that 40% of AI data centers will be power-constrained by 2027 due to lengthy grid connection approval timelines of 24 to 36 months in key markets such as Northern Virginia, Silicon Valley, and Northern Europe. The shift from hardware scarcity to power limitations is driven by the high electricity demand of AI workloads, especially inference, which operates continuously and accounts for an increasing share of energy consumption. Single data centers now require power capacities comparable to industrial facilities, with some planned sites needing 100 MW to 750 MW or more. This power constraint cannot be resolved by capital investment alone, prompting strategies focused on improving energy efficiency and tokens-per-watt performance to mitigate the impact while awaiting grid capacity expansion.

entry.title: Why Andreessen Horowitz's New Investor Left Apple [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Welcome, Weekenders! In this newsletter: • The Big Read: Trump's AI agenda collides with reality • Tech Culture: Welcome to the great private jet drought • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "Gastronomics," "Catch the Devil" and "The Invite" At the dawn of the AI boom, the technology sparked a real melee between newcomer startups and the industry's established giants. A good amount of the energy in that fight seems to have diminished lately, with the contest appearing to turn into a slugfest between a handful of heavyweights: Google, Anthropic and OpenAI in the lead, trailed by a few other contenders, like Meta Platforms and SpaceXAI. So that's it-the biggies will grab all the laurels? It's an outcome that has looked increasingly probable to me. Josh Elman, a longtime tech investor and executive, couldn't disagree more. And so staunch is his belief in a forthcoming boom in consumer AI startups that he jumped ship a few weeks ago from working on Apple's AI revamp to take up consumer investing at Andreessen Horowitz. Elman knows what he's getting into: Before Apple, he was a longtime Greylock partner, where he led its investments in companies like Discord, Musical.ly, the predecessor company of TikTok, and Meerkat, which became Houseparty before Epic Games bought it. And before Greylock, he worked at LinkedIn, Facebook and Twitter. To rebut my pessimism, Elman likened the current moment to the dot-com era's early days. "On the consumer adoption of AI, we're still back in 1995-maybe 1996," he said. My conversation with him, which has been edited for clarity and length, is below. First things first, I need to ask: Will Siri actually work now? Yes [laughs]. I think people have always wanted Siri just to be the thing that understands them and can help them just get stuff done on their device. I think it does great at that now. If you're gonna comp Siri to Claude Cowork and try to ask it: "Make me a crazy presentation on blah-blah-blah-blah," like, no-Siri's not designed to do that at this time. But if you do things like ask, "Call that Abe I was texting this morning," that works. And I do it all the time because I forget people's last names all the time. And here's another example: I was driving to dinner, and I was coming to Palo Alto, getting off at an exit, and there's two ways to go. I asked, "Navigate me to dinner with John." And then it took me right to the restaurant-even though I hadn't put the location on my calendar. We'd just texted about it. So why leave Apple now? AI seems to just be getting interesting there. What made you want to return to venture capital-and specifically to do consumer startups? When I left Greylock in 2020, I thought, "Consumer is dead. I don't know if you can do that anymore." And there have been a few companies, like Whatnot, which is an Andreessen company, and Suno. But there haven't been that many consumer AI companies. And the common wisdom has been that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and the model companies are going to define everything that's interesting in the next 10 years. What makes you so confident in defying that common wisdom? When OpenClaw came out six, seven months ago, I was like, "Oh, I get it again." The number of products that agentic AI can reinvent is going to lead to a Cambrian explosion that hasn't happened yet in consumer. And I think now's the window-now's the time. But I think of the OpenClaw craze as being pretty focused on a small, very Silicon Valley insider crowd who built work tools using it. Of all the amazing examples of OpenClaw use that were shared with me, I think about Claire Vo and Jesse Genet, who are moms who have been talking about how they use OpenClaw to manage their families and their kids. [Vo is the founder of ChatPRD; Genet is the CEO and co-founder of Lumi.com.] In the next six months, I think we're going to see the embers of exciting things coming out in consumer AI. I don't know exactly which ones will pop first. But two years from now, we're going to start to see things that are, you know, a set of agents that help you manage your life, and you'll be able to fine-tune them to accomplish what you want. Sure, consumer agents have real appeal. Won't the biggest companies with their established, giant relationships with consumers-Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, even Apple-just dominate that, too, though? Whether it's finance, travel, health-yes, a lot of us are already turning to ChatGPT or, like, Doctor Google. But there are going to be products that are much richer and much more experiential. And they're going to come from more than just those big players. If a startup was trying to say, "I'm going to be the primary coding assistant," well, that's a category that's fairly competitive now. There's at least five of them. But for travel, there certainly isn't anything yet. One of the things I learned at Apple is: No matter how ambitious and big you are as a company, you can only do a number of things well. And you would rather do a number of things really, really, really well rather than try to do all the things. At some point, that gap between the number of things they can do really well and all the things possible leaves a lot of opportunity for everybody.-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read Trump's AI Agenda Collides With Reality How staff turnover, turf battles and clashing views have derailed the administration's anti-regulation vision. Tech Culture Private Jets Are Scarce. Blame the Gusher of AI Wealth Silicon Valley's enormous surge in riches has turbocharged the market for new and used planes, energizing startups that offer innovative ways to gain access to an aircraft. Listening: "Gastronomics" Alex Mayyasi, host of "Gastronomics," a new podcast about food, business and the business of food, comes as finely pedigreed as a Thomas Keller-trained chef. Mayyasi is a longtime contributor to NPR's "Planet Money" and earlier this year turned some of the show's wit and wisdom into a bestselling book. Now cooking solo in his own kitchen, so to speak, Mayyasi has been applying his wonkish curiosity to topics such as menu forecasting, the bargain grocery wars and the internet-altering consequences of the Domino's pizza tracker. I love a chance to rest my mind from thinking about how capitalism intersects with lines of code and instead turn it to the intricacies of private-label Cheerios and the commotion around gochujang chicken wings. As I'd expect from a "Planet Money" veteran, Mayyasi does a fine job of establishing parallels between food companies and restaurant businesses and what else is happening in the corporate world. And I can tell that Mayyasi, who was employee No. 3 at Priceonomics, a short-lived, Y Combinator-backed media startup, is a techie at heart just by how he neatly likened Aldi, the sharp-elbowed discount grocery store, to Quince-you know, the internet's sharp-elbowed discount cashmere store.-Abram Brown Reading: "Catch the Devil" by Pamela Colloff It is an idea as old as Adam and Eve: The devil can take many forms, many of them less obvious than one with cloven hooves. And there was nothing particularly remarkable in the figure of Paul Skalnik, a tubby schlub of a fellow whose down-home appearance belied his prodigious, decadeslong series of cons across the Gulf Coast. (A version of Skalnik would, in other words, make for an engrossing season of "True Detective.") Skalnik was a fraudster, a robber and a covert polygamist: He married nine women, wedding some of them simultaneously. He was also a rat, and he kept himself out of any truly lengthy prison time by constantly informing to the authorities. He bamboozled them, too, and his testimony put four men on death row. Skalnik's indefatigable villainy-and the government's own exacerbation of it-makes for a riveting yarn, one unspooled with great care and craft by Pamela Colloff, who has been telling such stories for "Texas Monthly" for many years. "Catch the Devil" is a chronicle of Skalnik's misdeeds and his life, with Colloff tracking down an aged Skalnik in a Corsicana, Texas, nursing home, urging him to recant his testimony and save the life of one man still facing the death penalty. Colloff's reporting is riveting true crime and a stern, well-documented plea for America's criminal justice system to rethink how it handles informants.-A.B. Watching: "The Invite" I'm often struck by how the same creative impulses animate both Hollywood and Silicon Valley: In each, you can find enormous success by simply improving on someone else's idea. "The Invite," a witty sex comedy directed by Olivia Wilde, who also co-stars, iterates on a story originally from Barcelona-born writer-director Cesc Gay, who made it into a play and then a 2020 Spanish film. (Swiss, Korean and French adaptations have followed; a Dutch one is slated for 2027.) Wilde's version retains the same basic premise: A rather unhip couple tries to enliven their faltering relationship by asking their free-spirited neighbors over to dinner. Wilde plays one of the squares: out-of-work Angela, who is married to Joe (Seth Rogen), a music professor. Their guests are therapist Piña (Penélope Cruz) and ex-firefighter Hawk (Edward Norton), and their ensuing evening together is a night of entendre, horniness and disappointment: Seldom has a botched soufflé been a better-used metaphor. A large portion of the film was improvised by Wilde and her co-stars, a testament to their collective talent for comedic timing. The score, cinematography and editing are excellent, too-establishing a sense of voyeuristic anxiousness, a cross of Alfred Hitchcock and Woody Allen. Suffice it to say, I expect "The Invite" will find itself a guest of honor at next year's Oscars; Rogen, as something like a frumpled, grown-up "Peanuts" character, will almost certainly get his first nomination. A quibble: Most of the plot takes place within the apartment owned by Angela and Joe, but the broader setting is San Francisco. It would've made much more sense to place it someplace else. I find it impossible to imagine anyone in modern San Francisco being so unfamiliar with polyamory.-A.B.

entry.title: Trump's AI Agenda Collides With Reality [ * ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: In January 2025, just three days after entering office for his second term, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that revoked many of the Biden administration's efforts on AI. The order was part of Trump's promise to take a light-touch approach to AI regulation, rolling back what he would later describe as his predecessor's attempt to "paralyze" the industry through its emphasis on safety. Flanked by venture investor David Sacks, who had joined the administration as the AI and crypto czar, Trump scratched his signature on the order and then turned to his new adviser. "That should take us to the forefront, right?" he asked Sacks at the Oval Office event. "Absolutely," Sacks responded. "We got to win." Nearly halfway into Trump's second term, though, his ambitious AI agenda has been upended. The advent of powerful frontier models like Anthropic's Mythos has fueled fears among everyone from banking executives to intelligence agencies that they could lead to cybersecurity catastrophes. Public sentiment toward AI has shifted dramatically amid concerns about the technology's impact on everything from jobs to electricity prices, prompting hundreds of states, cities and counties to pass data center moratoriums.

entry.title: Private Jets Are Scarce. Blame the Gusher of AI Wealth
entry.summary: After Bill Papariella, a Fort Lauderdale, Fla.-based entrepreneur, sold his private jet charter business for nearly $1 billion in 2022, he took it easy for a couple years. But as the number of ultrawealthy continued to climb in the U.S., another business idea struck him: a company that offered fractional jet ownership, like NetJets, but with a service designed as an even more premium product. Last October, he launched Bond, planning a private plane fleet with interiors lined in Loro Piana textiles, custom crystal from French brand Saint-Louis and cabin attendants on every flight. To give Bond a heightened sense of exclusivity, Papariella capped the company's initial membership at around 100 people, who pay between $1.1 million and $3.5 million a year depending on the aircraft. Its members have an average net worth of $500 million, and about 30% of them hail from Silicon Valley-founders, researchers and engineers at companies like xAI, Anthropic and OpenAI, many of them under the age of 34, Papariella said. (He wouldn't comment publicly on anyone's identity.) Flights on a fleet of 20 airplanes will begin in 2027. "The amount of influx we've had from the youth has been something I did not see coming," said Papariella, speaking from a yacht in the Mediterranean Sea recently. "That's only happened over the last two months."
